author: Hale Stewart
title: Technically Speaking For January 3
text:
More bad news from China: Tim Cook published a letter to investors that contained bearish commentary on emerging markets generally and China specifically. In a section titled "Emerging Market Challenges," Cook wrote [emphasis added]:
China’s economy began to slow in the second half of 2018. The government-reported GDP growth during the September quarter was the second lowest in the last 25 years. We believe the economic environment in China has been further impacted by rising trade tensions with the United States. As the climate of mounting uncertainty weighed on financial markets, the effects appeared to reach consumers as well, with traffic to our retail stores and our channel partners in China declining as the quarter progressed. And market data has shown that the contraction in Greater China’s smartphone market has been particularly sharp.
Corporate communications are meant to be "rah-rah;" it takes a great deal of negativity for a CEO to state things are bad. There is ample support for Cook's concern. Auto sales are dropping sharply ; real estate markets are weak ; the latest Markit Manufacturing PMI data showed a modest contraction for the first time in several years . Just as China helped to soften the blow from the 2008 financial crisis so too could it be the precipitating factor of the next recession.
The ISM manufacturing index had been a reliably bullish indicator for the last year. No more. The latest report contains a sharp 5.2 point decline in the composite number , lowering it to 54.1. This number had printed in the high 50s and lower 60s for the last year. New orders declined a sharp 11 points, sending that reading to a just positive 51.1. The anecdotal comments are littered with cautionary language (emphasis added):
“Growth appears to have stopped. Resources still focused on re-sourcing for U.S. tariff mitigation out of China.” (Computer & Electronic Products) “Brexit has become a problem due to labeling changes.” (Chemical Products) “Customer demand continues to decrease [due to] concerns about the economy and tariffs.” (Transportation Equipment) “Starting to see more and more inflationary increases for raw materials. Also, suppliers [are] forcing price increases due to tariffs.” (Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products) “The ongoing open issues with tariffs between U.S. and China are causing longer-term concerns about costs and sourcing strategies for our manufacturing operations. We were anticipating more clarity [regarding] tariffs at the end of 2018.” (Machinery) “Business is steady, but pace of incoming orders are slowing.” (Furniture & Related Products) “Business is robust for certain sectors [aerospace] and flat to downward for others [energy]. Tariffs continue to impact business direction and profit.” (Miscellaneous Manufacturing) “Caution seems to be the outlook. Are we in a correction, or is the market getting ready to slow over time?” (Fabricated Metal Products) “No major change in business operations towards the end of 2018; however, we are carefully monitoring oil prices and outside influence from market conditions to better understand our 2019 outlook and capital plans.” (Petroleum & Coal Products) “Customers are hedge buying in December as a result of announced price increases starting in January.” (Textile Mills) This report's internals show that several macro events are hurting manufacturing. Caution is warranted.
Today, White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett commented , " It's not going to be just Apple ... There are a heck of a lot of U.S. companies that have sales in China that are going to be watching their earnings being downgraded next year until we get a deal with China.” While seasoned investors won't be phased by these comments (in fact, they probably agree with the assessment), it was an unfortunate comment to make.
Let's look at a few daily summaries, starting with the major index ETFs:
The long-end of the yield curve was the top performer, with the TLT rising 1.15% and the TLHs advancing .84%. The rest of the curve was modestly higher. It gets ugly after that. The transport index was the worst performer -- this sector sells across the globe, making Apple's negative Chinese assessment a sign of slower sales. AAPL and the tech sector brought QQQ down nearly 3.5%. Oddly, the smaller caps did fairly well (relatively speaking); the micro and small-cap indexes were off less than 2%.
The sector orientation was bearish: real estate, utilities, and staples were the top three performers. Healthcare was the fifth best. To no one's surprise, tech was down slightly more than 5%. However, all sectors suffered.
The heat map from Finviz.com shows a ton of red. Biotech caught a bid thanks to the BMY/Celgene deal. REITs were modestly higher and utilities were close to break-even. Aside from that, it's ugly.
The charts are less-than encouraging:
Today, we had three separate rallies. Prices couldn't get meaningfully beyond the 200-minute EMA, which turned lower after lunch and continued down through the close. Prices also closed near the daily low -- which is never an encouraging sign. Prices traded in a narrow range over the holidays. This morning, prices broke support, tried to rally, and then continued lower. Notice all the EMAs are moving lower.
On the 2-week chart, prices were trading in the upper Fibonacci zones over the new year. Now, they're moving lower, although they still have Fib support. Notice that momentum has been declining since December 28.
Prices can't get beyond the 200-minute EMA on the 30-day chart.
And finally, on the daily chart prices hit resistance at February lows and are now moving lower.
You'll notice that there was a complete lack of any bullish commentary across multiple time zones. That's because the bearish tenor of the market has carried over from last year. The market needs to find a bottom. It just hasn't made a decision about where that is yet.
